Good
GOOD
adj. and n. (conformed to the character and will of God; beneficial, upright, excellent; rendering Hebrew tōb and Greek agathos, kalos)
From Old English gōd, common Germanic, fitting or suitable — the underlying idea being a thing answering to its purpose. English God and good are not etymologically related, a coincidence of spelling only, though the theology binds them tightly enough. Hebrew tōb covers moral goodness, beauty, pleasantness, and practical usefulness in one word, which is why Gen 1 can pronounce the creation good without distinguishing the aesthetic from the ethical. Greek divides the ground: agathos is good in nature and effect, kalos good as beautiful, noble, and fit to be seen.

Biblical Definition

Good is not an independent standard by which God may be measured; it is a description of what God is, and derivatively of what conforms to Him. Creation's goodness is a verdict He pronounces: “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31). Matter, sex, food, work, and the body are therefore good by divine declaration, and every asceticism that treats them as inherently defiling is corrected at the first page. The Lord Jesus fixes the term's ultimate reference in a single sentence to a man who used it flatteringly: “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God” (Mar 10:18) — not a denial of His own deity but a refusal to let the word float free of it. What God requires of man is likewise not obscure: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good” (Mic 6:8), and the content is justice, mercy, and humble walking. And because God is good, He is trustworthy in the dark: “O taste and see that the LORD is good” (Psa 34:8) is an invitation to experiment on His character, and Rom 8:28 extends the verdict over everything that happens to those who love Him. Good works follow salvation as its fruit and never precede it as its price (Eph 2:8–10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Conformed to the character and will of God; in Scripture the verdict God pronounces on His creation, the description of His own nature, the summary of what He requires of man, and the fruit — never the ground — of salvation.

expand to see more

GOOD, a. 1. Valid; legally firm; not weak or defective; having strength adequate to its support; as a good title.

2. Valuable; useful; not bad, hurtful or pernicious; as, good fruit; a good tree.

3. Conformable to the moral law; virtuous; applied to actions. In this sense it is equivalent to right.

4. Complete or sufficiently perfect in its kind; having the physical qualities best adapted to its design and use; as good timber; a good soil.

5. GOOD, n. That which contributes to diminish or remove pain, or to increase happiness or prosperity; benefit; advantage. In theology, the chief good is God Himself, in whose enjoyment the creature's blessedness consists — the summum bonum of the older divines.

Key Scripture

Gen 1:31 — "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day."

Psa 34:8 — "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him."

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Mar 10:18 — "And Jesus said unto him, Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God."

Modern Corruption

Moral relativism detaches good from God and reduces it to preference or social consensus, so that the word survives while its standard is gone; and Mic 6:8 is regularly quoted as a programme of social action with its third clause — walking humbly with thy God — quietly dropped.

expand to see more

Once good is severed from God it can only mean what a person or a culture approves, and the word becomes a container for whatever is currently applauded. The Lord Jesus refused this move in advance: there is none good but one, that is, God. Goodness is not a standard external to Him that He happens to meet, nor an arbitrary decree He might have issued otherwise; it is His nature, and the moral law is its published expression. This is why a society can retain the vocabulary of good and evil long after it has abandoned any means of adjudicating between them, and why appeals to decency grow shriller as the ground for them erodes.

The second corruption is a selective quotation. Mic 6:8 is among the most-cited verses in progressive religious advocacy, invariably in the form “do justice, love mercy” — and just as invariably without “walk humbly with thy God,” which is the clause that makes the other two possible and defines them. Micah is not proposing an ethical programme detachable from the God who shewed it; he is rebuking a nation that offered sacrifices instead of obedience. Justice defined by anything other than God's revealed law becomes whatever the strongest party calls justice. The Reformed reading keeps all three clauses and keeps them in order.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tōb (good in every register — moral, aesthetic, useful, pleasant), the verdict word of Gen 1; Greek agathos (good in nature and effect) and kalos (good as beautiful and fit), which divide between them what Hebrew held in one.

expand to see more

tōb (Hebrew, H2896) — good, pleasant, agreeable, morally right; the verdict repeated seven times in Gen 1 and intensified at v. 31, and the word in “it is not good that the man should be alone.”

agathos (Greek, G18) — good in nature and in effect; the word in Rom 8:28 and in Eph 2:10, “created in Christ Jesus unto good works.”

kalos (Greek, G2570) — good as noble, beautiful, and fit to be seen; the word in Mat 5:16 (“that they may see your good works”) and in “the good shepherd” of Joh 10:11, where the shepherd is not merely effective but admirable.

summum bonum (Latin) — the highest good; the scholastic and Puritan term for God Himself as the creature's final blessedness, and the frame behind the Westminster Shorter Catechism's first answer.

1689 London Baptist Confession 16.1–3 — good works are only such as God hath commanded in His holy word, done in obedience to it, and wrought by the Spirit; the confessional guard against both moralism and antinomianism.

Usage

"Gen 1:31 is the church's standing answer to every form of Gnosticism: the material creation is not a fall from something purer but a thing God looked at and called very good."

"Mar 10:18 is often misread as a disclaimer of deity. The logic runs the other way — the ruler is being asked whether he knows what he has just called Jesus, and the question is left standing."

"The Hebrew tōb refuses the modern separation of the beautiful from the right. A Reformed aesthetic begins here: what is genuinely good is also, in its own order, fitting and lovely."
